title: A five-team football league
intro: Five teams A, B, C, D and E played a round-robin league: every team played every other team exactly once. A win earned 3 points, a draw 1 point and a loss 0.
It is also known that A and B did not lose any match, and D's only point came from its match against B.

qs.s: How many matches ended in a draw?
qs.e: Total points = 8 + 8 + 6 + 1 + 4 = 27. A decisive match gives 3 points in total and a draw 2. With 10 matches: 3W + 2D = 27 and W + D = 10 → D = 3.

qs.s: What was the result of the match between A and E?
qs.e: Unbeaten with 8 points means 2 wins + 2 draws, for both A and B, and A–B must be a draw. D's only point is the draw with B, so D lost to A, C and E, and B beat C and E. A's other draw is with C or E. If A drew with C, C (beaten by B, winner over D) would need 2 more points from its match with E — impossible. So A beat C and drew with E.

qs.s: How many matches did C win?
qs.e: C's 6 points with no draw available against A or B (they beat C) means two wins: over D and E.

qs.s: Which team did E defeat?
qs.e: E's 4 points = a draw with A + a win. E lost to B and C, so the win must be over D.

title: Six friends in a row
intro: Six friends P, Q, R, S, T and U sit in a row of six seats numbered 1 to 6 from left to right, all facing the same direction.

1. P sits at one of the two ends.
2. Q sits immediately to the right of R.
3. S does not sit next to P.
4. T sits in seat 3 or seat 4.
5. U sits to the left of S with exactly one person between them.
6. R sits to the right of T.

qs.s: Who sits in seat 1?
qs.e: T is in seat 3 or 4, and R–Q (adjacent, Q on the right) sit to the right of T. If P were in seat 6, R–Q would need seats 4–5 with T in 3, leaving seats 1–2 for U and S — but they need exactly one seat between them. So P is in seat 1. If T were in 4, R–Q take 5–6 and U, S get seats 2–3, again no gap. Hence T is in 3, R–Q in 5–6, and U, S in seats 2 and 4. Final order: P, U, T, S, R, Q.

qs.s: Who sits immediately to the left of S?
qs.e: T is in seat 3 or 4, and R–Q (adjacent, Q on the right) sit to the right of T. If P were in seat 6, R–Q would need seats 4–5 with T in 3, leaving seats 1–2 for U and S — but they need exactly one seat between them. So P is in seat 1. If T were in 4, R–Q take 5–6 and U, S get seats 2–3, again no gap. Hence T is in 3, R–Q in 5–6, and U, S in seats 2 and 4. Final order: P, U, T, S, R, Q.

qs.s: In which seat does T sit?
qs.e: T is in seat 3 or 4, and R–Q (adjacent, Q on the right) sit to the right of T. If P were in seat 6, R–Q would need seats 4–5 with T in 3, leaving seats 1–2 for U and S — but they need exactly one seat between them. So P is in seat 1. If T were in 4, R–Q take 5–6 and U, S get seats 2–3, again no gap. Hence T is in 3, R–Q in 5–6, and U, S in seats 2 and 4. Final order: P, U, T, S, R, Q.

qs.s: How many people sit between P and U?
qs.e: T is in seat 3 or 4, and R–Q (adjacent, Q on the right) sit to the right of T. If P were in seat 6, R–Q would need seats 4–5 with T in 3, leaving seats 1–2 for U and S — but they need exactly one seat between them. So P is in seat 1. If T were in 4, R–Q take 5–6 and U, S get seats 2–3, again no gap. Hence T is in 3, R–Q in 5–6, and U, S in seats 2 and 4. Final order: P, U, T, S, R, Q.

title: A week of guest lectures
intro: Five professors — Iyer, Jain, Kapoor, Lal and Menon — each deliver one lecture, on five different subjects (Maths, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, English), one lecture per day from Monday to Friday.

1. Maths is on Wednesday.
2. Physics is on the day immediately after Chemistry.
3. Iyer lectures on Monday, but not on English.
4. Kapoor lectures on Biology.
5. Lal lectures earlier in the week than Kapoor.
6. Menon lectures on Friday.

qs.s: On which day is the Biology lecture?
qs.e: Wednesday is Maths, so Chemistry–Physics fall on Mon–Tue or Thu–Fri. Kapoor (Biology) cannot be on Monday (Iyer), Wednesday (Maths) or Friday (Menon). If Kapoor were on Tuesday, Lal would have to lecture on Monday — Iyer's day. So Kapoor lectures Biology on Thursday, which pushes Chemistry–Physics to Monday–Tuesday and leaves English for Friday. Iyer (Monday) takes Chemistry. Jain and Lal share Tuesday and Wednesday; Jain can't take Maths, so Jain has Tuesday (Physics) and Lal Wednesday (Maths).

qs.e: Wednesday is Maths, so Chemistry–Physics fall on Mon–Tue or Thu–Fri. Kapoor (Biology) cannot be on Monday (Iyer), Wednesday (Maths) or Friday (Menon). qs.e: Wednesday is Maths, so Chemistry–Physics fall on Mon–Tue or Thu–Fri. Kapoor (Biology) cannot be on Monday (Iyer), Wednesday (Maths) or Friday (Menon). Iyer (Monday) takes Chemistry. Jain and Lal share Tuesday and Wednesday; Jain can't take Maths, so Jain has Tuesday (Physics) and Lal Wednesday (Maths).

qs.s: On which day does Jain lecture?
qs.e: Wednesday is Maths, so Chemistry–Physics fall on Mon–Tue or Thu–Fri. Kapoor (Biology) cannot be on Monday (Iyer), Wednesday (Maths) or Friday (Menon). If Kapoor were on Tuesday, Lal would have to lecture on Monday — Iyer's day. So Kapoor lectures Biology on Thursday, which pushes Chemistry–Physics to Monday–Tuesday and leaves English for Friday. Iyer (Monday) takes Chemistry. Jain and Lal share Tuesday and Wednesday; Jain can't take Maths, so Jain has Tuesday (Physics) and Lal Wednesday (Maths).

title: Sharing 30 chocolates
intro: Thirty chocolates were distributed among four children W, X, Y and Z. Each child got at least 3 chocolates and no two children got the same number.

1. X got twice as many chocolates as W.
2. Y got 4 more chocolates than Z.
3. Z got more chocolates than W.
4. Y got more chocolates than X.

qs.s: How many chocolates did W get?
qs.e: Write W = w, X = 2w, Z = z, Y = z + 4. Then w + 2w + z + z + 4 = 30 → 3w + 2z = 26, so w is even. w = 4 gives z = 7 (and z > w ✓); w = 6 gives z = 4 (fails z > w); w ≥ 8 makes z too small. So W = 4, X = 8, Z = 7, Y = 11 — and Y > X holds.

qs.s: How many chocolates did Y get?
qs.e: Write W = w, X = 2w, Z = z, Y = z + 4. Then w + 2w + z + z + 4 = 30 → 3w + 2z = 26, so w is even. w = 4 gives z = 7 (and z > w ✓); w = 6 gives z = 4 (fails z > w); w ≥ 8 makes z too small. So W = 4, X = 8, Z = 7, Y = 11 — and Y > X holds.

qs.s: Who got the second-highest number of chocolates?
qs.e: Write W = w, X = 2w, Z = z, Y = z + 4. Then w + 2w + z + z + 4 = 30 → 3w + 2z = 26, so w is even. w = 4 gives z = 7 (and z > w ✓); w = 6 gives z = 4 (fails z > w); w ≥ 8 makes z too small. So W = 4, X = 8, Z = 7, Y = 11 — and Y > X holds.

qs.s: What is the difference between the largest and the smallest share?
qs.e: Write W = w, X = 2w, Z = z, Y = z + 4. Then w + 2w + z + z + 4 = 30 → 3w + 2z = 26, so w is even. w = 4 gives z = 7 (and z > w ✓); w = 6 gives z = 4 (fails z > w); w ≥ 8 makes z too small. So W = 4, X = 8, Z = 7, Y = 11 — and Y > X holds.

title: Languages spoken by 220 employees
intro: In an office of 220 employees, each employee speaks some of Hindi, English and Tamil, or none of them.

Exactly two: Hindi–English only 25 − 5 = 20, Hindi–Tamil only 17 − 5 = 12, English–Tamil only 13 − 5 = 8. title: Three races, five runners
intro: Five runners V, W, X, Y and Z ran three races. In each race the finishing positions 1st to 5th earned 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 points respectively; there were no ties.

1. V won the first race but finished last in the second.
2. The three races had three different winners; Z won the third race.
3. X finished second in both the second and the third race.
4. Y finished last in the third race, in which W finished ahead of V.
5. In the first race, Y finished ahead of X.
6. The final totals were 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7 points; W scored 11 and X scored 10.

qs.s: What was V's total score?
qs.e: X was 2nd in races 2 and 3 (4 + 4) and scored 10 in all, so X was 4th in race 1. In race 3: Z 1st, X 2nd, Y 5th, and W ahead of V → W 3rd, V 4th. W scored 11, so W got 8 from races 1 and 2. Race 2's winner is not V or Z (three different winners). If Y won race 2, W would be at most 3rd there and would need 5+ points in race 1 — impossible, as V won it. So W won race 2 and was 3rd in race 1. Race 1: V, then Y ahead of X → Y 2nd, Z 5th. V = 5 + 1 + 2 = 8. Totals 9 and 7 remain for Y and Z: Y = 4 + (race 2) + 1, Z = 1 + (race 2) + 5, with race-2 points 3 and 2 between them → Y = 7, Z = 9 (Z 3rd, Y 4th in race 2).

qs.s: Who won the second race?
qs.e: X was 2nd in races 2 and 3 (4 + 4) and scored 10 in all, so X was 4th in race 1. In race 3: Z 1st, X 2nd, Y 5th, and W ahead of V → W 3rd, V 4th. W scored 11, so W got 8 from races 1 and 2. Race 2's winner is not V or Z (three different winners). If Y won race 2, W would be at most 3rd there and would need 5+ points in race 1 — impossible, as V won it. So W won race 2 and was 3rd in race 1. Race 1: V, then Y ahead of X → Y 2nd, Z 5th. V = 5 + 1 + 2 = 8. Totals 9 and 7 remain for Y and Z: Y = 4 + (race 2) + 1, Z = 1 + (race 2) + 5, with race-2 points 3 and 2 between them → Y = 7, Z = 9 (Z 3rd, Y 4th in race 2).

qs.s: How many points did Z score in total?
qs.e: X was 2nd in races 2 and 3 (4 + 4) and scored 10 in all, so X was 4th in race 1. In race 3: Z 1st, X 2nd, Y 5th, and W ahead of V → W 3rd, V 4th. W scored 11, so W got 8 from races 1 and 2. Race 2's winner is not V or Z (three different winners). If Y won race 2, W would be at most 3rd there and would need 5+ points in race 1 — impossible, as V won it. So W won race 2 and was 3rd in race 1. Race 1: V, then Y ahead of X → Y 2nd, Z 5th. V = 5 + 1 + 2 = 8. Totals 9 and 7 remain for Y and Z: Y = 4 + (race 2) + 1, Z = 1 + (race 2) + 5, with race-2 points 3 and 2 between them → Y = 7, Z = 9 (Z 3rd, Y 4th in race 2).

qs.s: What was Y's position in the second race?
qs.e: X was 2nd in races 2 and 3 (4 + 4) and scored 10 in all, so X was 4th in race 1. In race 3: Z 1st, X 2nd, Y 5th, and W ahead of V → W 3rd, V 4th. W scored 11, so W got 8 from races 1 and 2. Race 2's winner is not V or Z (three different winners). If Y won race 2, W would be at most 3rd there and would need 5+ points in race 1 — impossible, as V won it. So W won race 2 and was 3rd in race 1. Race 1: V, then Y ahead of X → Y 2nd, Z 5th. V = 5 + 1 + 2 = 8. Totals 9 and 7 remain for Y and Z: Y = 4 + (race 2) + 1, Z = 1 + (race 2) + 5, with race-2 points 3 and 2 between them → Y = 7, Z = 9 (Z 3rd, Y 4th in race 2).

title: Ages of six classmates
intro: Six classmates — Anu, Bala, Chitra, Dev, Esha and Farhan — have six different ages, which are the integers from 21 to 26.

1. Anu's age plus Bala's age equals Chitra's age plus Dev's age.
2. Esha is exactly 3 years older than Farhan.
3. Anu is older than Esha.
4. Dev's age is an even number.
5. Chitra is younger than Dev.
6. Farhan is not the youngest.

qs.s: What is Anu's age?
qs.e: Esha = Farhan + 3 and Anu is older than Esha, so (Farhan, Esha) is (21, 24) or (22, 25) — (23, 26) leaves no older age for Anu. Farhan is not the youngest, so Farhan = 22, Esha = 25 and Anu = 26. Bala, Chitra and Dev share 21, 23 and 24; Dev is even → 24. Clue 1: 26 + Bala = Chitra + 24 → Chitra = Bala + 2 → Bala = 21, Chitra = 23 (and Chitra < Dev ✓).

qs.s: Who is the youngest?
qs.e: Esha = Farhan + 3 and Anu is older than Esha, so (Farhan, Esha) is (21, 24) or (22, 25) — (23, 26) leaves no older age for Anu. Farhan is not the youngest, so Farhan = 22, Esha = 25 and Anu = 26. Bala, Chitra and Dev share 21, 23 and 24; Dev is even → 24. Clue 1: 26 + Bala = Chitra + 24 → Chitra = Bala + 2 → Bala = 21, Chitra = 23 (and Chitra < Dev ✓).

qs.s: What is the sum of Bala's and Chitra's ages?
qs.e: Esha = Farhan + 3 and Anu is older than Esha, so (Farhan, Esha) is (21, 24) or (22, 25) — (23, 26) leaves no older age for Anu. Farhan is not the youngest, so Farhan = 22, Esha = 25 and Anu = 26. Bala, Chitra and Dev share 21, 23 and 24; Dev is even → 24. Clue 1: 26 + Bala = Chitra + 24 → Chitra = Bala + 2 → Bala = 21, Chitra = 23 (and Chitra < Dev ✓).

qs.s: How many classmates are older than Chitra?
qs.e: Esha = Farhan + 3 and Anu is older than Esha, so (Farhan, Esha) is (21, 24) or (22, 25) — (23, 26) leaves no older age for Anu. Farhan is not the youngest, so Farhan = 22, Esha = 25 and Anu = 26. Bala, Chitra and Dev share 21, 23 and 24; Dev is even → 24. Clue 1: 26 + Bala = Chitra + 24 → Chitra = Bala + 2 → Bala = 21, Chitra = 23 (and Chitra < Dev ✓).

title: A 3 × 3 number grid
intro: The digits 1 to 9 are placed in a 3 × 3 grid, one digit per cell, so that every row, every column and both main diagonals add up to the same total.

Rows are numbered 1–3 from top to bottom and columns 1–3 from left to right.
1. The digit in row 1, column 1 is 2.
2. In row 1, the middle digit is larger than the right-hand digit.
3. The digit in row 3, column 2 is greater than 2.

qs.s: What digit is in the centre of the grid?
qs.e: All digits add to 45, so every line adds to 15. The four lines through the centre add to 4 × 15 = 60 = 45 + 3 × centre → centre = 5. Diagonal: 2 + 5 + (row 3, col 3) = 15 → 8. Row 1: 2 + a + b = 15 with a > b → (a, b) = (9, 4) or (7, 6). Column 2: a + 5 + c = 15 → c = 10 − a, and c > 2 → a = 7, b = 6, c = 3. The rest follows: rows (2, 7, 6), (9, 5, 1), (4, 3, 8).

qs.s: What digit is in row 3, column 3?
qs.e: All digits add to 45, so every line adds to 15. The four lines through the centre add to 4 × 15 = 60 = 45 + 3 × centre → centre = 5. Diagonal: 2 + 5 + (row 3, col 3) = 15 → 8. Row 1: 2 + a + b = 15 with a > b → (a, b) = (9, 4) or (7, 6). Column 2: a + 5 + c = 15 → c = 10 − a, and c > 2 → a = 7, b = 6, c = 3. The rest follows: rows (2, 7, 6), (9, 5, 1), (4, 3, 8).

qs.s: What digit is in row 1, column 2?
qs.e: All digits add to 45, so every line adds to 15. The four lines through the centre add to 4 × 15 = 60 = 45 + 3 × centre → centre = 5. Diagonal: 2 + 5 + (row 3, col 3) = 15 → 8. Row 1: 2 + a + b = 15 with a > b → (a, b) = (9, 4) or (7, 6). Column 2: a + 5 + c = 15 → c = 10 − a, and c > 2 → a = 7, b = 6, c = 3. The rest follows: rows (2, 7, 6), (9, 5, 1), (4, 3, 8).

qs.s: What is the digit in row 2, column 1?
qs.e: All digits add to 45, so every line adds to 15. The four lines through the centre add to 4 × 15 = 60 = 45 + 3 × centre → centre = 5. Diagonal: 2 + 5 + (row 3, col 3) = 15 → 8. Row 1: 2 + a + b = 15 with a > b → (a, b) = (9, 4) or (7, 6). Column 2: a + 5 + c = 15 → c = 10 − a, and c > 2 → a = 7, b = 6, c = 3. The rest follows: rows (2, 7, 6), (9, 5, 1), (4, 3, 8).
